alternatives.concept: Study comparative private, public, criminal, European and international law through cases, legal sources and reasoned advice. Business finance, ethics, empirical research and negotiation connect legal questions to transactions, institutions and conflict prevention. This broader programme responds to the confirmed first-two-year legal core; it does not reproduce the Dutch notarial, family, company, property or tax-law sequence.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Legal traditions, case briefs, IRAC and public/private-law foundations address the introductory legal inquiry; Dutch doctrinal details differ.
Treaties, responsibility, jurisdiction, international institutions and case analysis supply substantive public-international-law correspondence.
Comparative constitutional institutions, rights and judicial review address identifiable constitutional-law substance; no complete Dutch public-law equivalence.

Actual contract formation, interpretation, fairness, performance and remedies directly address an important part of ObligationsI. The one comparative module also includes property/tort; it does not replace the external full Dutch sequence.
Natural-law/positivist foundations, rights justification and legal-philosophical argument address a defined part of jurisprudence; not the whole external philosophical canon.

Actual intellectual-property and contractual-remedy advisory work addresses an identifiable part of ObligationsII, which combines liability and IP. This partial relationship does not establish its complete Dutch tort/risk-liability curriculum.
Criminal liability, legality, defences, punishment and hypothetical legal advice directly address criminal-law foundations; jurisdiction-specific doctrine differs.
EU legal effect, judicial remedies, citizenship and free-movement case work directly address the substantive European-law strand; detailed competition/national applications differ.

Financial statements, corporate-finance and discounted-cash-flow/investment analysis directly address the important accounting and valuation functions in BusinessEconomics; UCR does not teach notarial financial-professional rules.

Ethical analysis of AI, responsibility, fairness and human-technology relations addresses an important identifiable part of technology-and-law inquiry. It does not reproduce the external Heidegger/Weber/Nietzsche approach or legal doctrine.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Notarial Law degree develops a broad foundation in Dutch, European and international law, followed by specialist study of property, family and company law. Students learn to research legal questions, interpret legal sources and build legal arguments.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This comparison assesses the confirmed first two years of Leiden’s revised Notarial Law degree. UCR can offer sustained comparative legal study combined with business finance, ethical judgment and reasoned advice. It provides less Dutch private-law depth and does not reproduce the known family, company, property or tax-law sequence. The third-year specialization, thesis and full degree progression are excluded from the comparison.

curriculum.limitation: The 125 EC shown comprise 110 EC of named first-two-year study, 10 EC of second-year electives and 5 EC of third-year electives. This comparison assesses the confirmed first two years, with no elective contents assumed. All 60 EC of third-year formation, including the unknown 55 EC of required study and thesis, are excluded from the academic comparison. The full 180-EC pathway and cohort progression are not certified.

componentNotes.not1-01: Alongside the credited first-year courses, students must complete Leiden Law Practices tutoring and pass the legal Dutch language test to complete the first-year examination. These compulsory activities carry 0 EC and do not add to the displayed credits.
componentNotes.not1-06: Builds on Introduction to Private Law I.
componentNotes.not2-01: Entry requires Introduction to Administrative Law; the course builds on its concepts and legal-remedy framework.
componentNotes.not2-02: Entry requires Introduction to Private Law I in the revised curriculum.
componentNotes.not2-03: Entry requires first-year Introduction to European Law.
componentNotes.not2-04: Entry requires Introduction to Private Law I in the revised curriculum.
componentNotes.not2-05: Entry requires both Introduction to Private Law I and II. The course also builds on the law of obligations.
componentNotes.not2-07: Entry requires both Introduction to Private Law I and II. This course excludes marital property law, which is a separate specialist subject.
componentNotes.not2-08: Presupposes a sound understanding of basic obligations and property-law principles.
componentNotes.not2-10: One of three approved 5 EC technology-and-law options. This example uses Philosophy of Technology and Law; students do not take all three for these credits.
componentNotes.not2-11: 10 EC of the programme’s 15 EC elective allowance; the other 5 EC is in year three. Individual elective courses must each carry at least 5 EC. For courses taken within the Law Faculty, the full allowance includes 10 EC at level 200 or above and 5 EC at level 300 or above. Courses must avoid overlap with compulsory study; Honours College courses cannot count. Approval rules apply, with exceptions for recognized minors and Leiden courses meeting the conditions. A 30 EC minor is not automatically counted within this 15 EC allowance.
componentNotes.not3-elective-space-5: The remaining 5 EC of the 15 EC programme elective allowance, placed in year three. The same level, overlap and approval conditions apply as to the second-year elective space. This verified category does not establish the rest of the revised third-year curriculum.

comparisonScope.label: Qualified academic-core comparison
comparisonScope.assessed: The first 120 EC: 110 EC of named legal, financial and technology-law study plus 10 EC of genuine electives with no assumed contents. All 125 documented EC remain visible; the additional 5-EC third-year elective category is outside the assessed core.
comparisonScope.excluded: All 60 EC of third-year academic formation, including the 5-EC displayed elective category and 55 EC of unverified required study, thesis and final training. Full notarial-degree comparability, graduation access and future progression are not certified.

acceptance.claim: A complete feasible UCR legal-business programme meaningfully responds to the confirmed first-two-year NotarialLaw academic core through actual comparative private/public/EU/international/criminal/rights law, commercial transactions, financial analysis, ethics and empirical legal inquiry. Known Dutch private-law, family/company/property and statutory-tax differences remain. This is not a comparison of the revised third-year specialization, thesis, full degree or professional preparation.
